items.d: 247 recommendations on Centre-state relations: use **Article 356 as a last resort** and only after a warning, appoint the Governor from **outside the state and not a recent politician** and in **consultation with the Chief Minister**, make the **Inter-State Council under Article 263 a permanent body** (done in 1990), and consult states before legislating on Concurrent List subjects.

Went further: a **fixed five-year tenure for Governors** and removal only by **impeachment-like process by the state legislature**, appointment from a **panel prepared by the state**, **'localised' President's Rule** confined to a district or region rather than the whole state, a **Superintendence-free CBI requiring state consent**, and an amendment to Article 355 to define the Union's duty to protect states.

Set up by Tamil Nadu — the first substantial state-side critique: **abolish Articles 356, 357 and 365**, make the **Finance Commission a permanent body**, transfer subjects from the Union to the State List, and constitute an **Inter-State Council** at once. The founding document of the state-autonomy demand.

**15th FC (N.K. Singh)**: states' share **41%**, horizontal criteria — income distance 45%, area 15%, population (2011) 15%, demographic performance 12.5%, forest and ecology 10%, tax effort 2.5%; a separate **defence and internal security fund**. **16th FC (Arvind Panagariya)**, whose award runs **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031**, kept the states' share at **41%**, rejecting the 50% many states demanded; introduced a **10% weight for contribution to GDP** and **dropped the tax-and-fiscal-effort criterion**; recommended the Centre cut its fiscal deficit to **3.5% by 2030-31** and states hold to **3% of GSDP**; and pressed for **off-budget borrowing by states to be discontinued and brought on-budget**. Finance Commission grants for FY27 are about **₹1.4 lakh crore**, including local body and disaster management grants.

On panchayati raj: recommended a **two-tier system (Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat)**, made the **Zila Parishad the pivot** of planning, allowed **open participation of political parties**, and proposed compulsory taxation powers and reservation for SC/ST. Its logic underlies the 73rd Amendment even though the two-tier design was not adopted.

Recommended **'democratic decentralisation'** and the **three-tier structure** — Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti (the executive body) and Zila Parishad (advisory and supervisory), with the **Block as the unit** and genuine transfer of resources. Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959) implemented it first, followed by Andhra Pradesh.

First to recommend **constitutional status for panchayati raj**, the **gram sabha as the embodiment of direct democracy**, **nyaya panchayats** for judicial functions, and **regular elections through a State Election Commission** — the intellectual blueprint of the 73rd Amendment.

On Telangana — examined six options and became the reference document for the **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014**. Pair with the **Fazl Ali States Reorganisation Commission (1955)** — which rejected language as the *sole* basis but produced the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956** and 14 states plus 6 UTs — and the **Dhar Commission (1948)** and **JVP Committee (1949)**, which had opposed linguistic states.

**15 reports**. Signature recommendations: the **Right to Information as the master key to good governance** (1st), **Ethics in Governance** — a National Ombudsman, state funding of elections, partial disqualification on framing of charges (4th), **Local Governance** with 'a total transfer of functions, functionaries and funds' (6th), **Capacity Building for Conflict Resolution** (7th), a **Public Services Bill and a Central Civil Services Authority** (10th), and 'Refurbishing of Personnel Administration' (10th). The default citation for any governance reform answer.

items.t: First ARC (1966-70, Morarji Desai then K. Hanumanthaiya)
items.d: 20 reports; recommended **Lokpal and Lokayukta** (the origin of the idea in India), the creation of a **Department of Personnel** outside ministries, and specialisation in the civil services through mid-career streaming.

On the prevention of corruption — produced the **Central Vigilance Commission** and the vigilance-officer network, and identified the 'four-fold' sources of corruption in administrative delay, scarcity, cumbersome procedures and discretion.

On electoral reform: **state funding in kind**, **disqualification for booth capturing**, **a single election commission decision on disqualification under Art. 103/192 to follow the ECI's opinion**, restricting the anti-defection law to a vote of confidence and money bills, and the appointment of the CEC in consultation with the CJI and the Leader of Opposition.

On **state funding of elections** — recommended it **in kind and only for recognised parties and their candidates**, and only once **internal party democracy and audited accounts** are in place. Cite alongside the **Law Commission's 255th Report (2015)** on electoral reform and the **170th Report (1999)** on internal party democracy and the two-ballot system.

On the **criminal-politician-bureaucrat nexus** — found that crime syndicates had developed a 'network of muscle-power, money-power and patronage' and had begun to enjoy political protection; recommended a nodal agency to collate intelligence. The founding official acknowledgement of criminalisation of politics.

On **'One Nation, One Election'** — recommended simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly elections in the **first step**, and local body elections **within 100 days** in the second; a **single electoral roll and single voter ID**; and constitutional amendments to Articles 82A, 83, 172 and 324A, some requiring **state ratification**. Objections: federalism, the fate of a House that falls mid-term, and the national-issue dominance over state issues.

items.t: T.S.R. Subramanian Committee (2013 judgment; 2016 education committee)
items.d: The **service-reform directions** (Civil Services Board, fixed tenure, written orders) came from the Supreme Court in *T.S.R. Subramanian*. The **separate T.S.R. Subramanian Committee (2016)** on the New Education Policy preceded the **K. Kasturirangan Committee (2019)**, whose draft became **NEP 2020**.

Constituted after the December 2012 Delhi gang rape, reported in **29 days**: widened the definition of rape, recommended criminalising **marital rape** (not accepted), **stalking, voyeurism and acid attacks** as offences, punishment for **police failure to register an FIR**, and rejected the death penalty and lowering the juvenile age. Produced the **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013**.

items.t: Punchhi and Malimath on criminal justice
items.d: The **Malimath Committee (2003)** recommended shifting from adversarial towards a **partly inquisitorial** system, a lower standard of proof ('clear and convincing'), a **victim's right to participate and to compensation**, and a National Judicial Commission. The **Madhav Menon Committee (2007)** drafted the National Policy on Criminal Justice.

On the social, economic and educational status of Muslims — found their conditions **below the national average and in some respects below SC/STs**, coined the phrase that Muslims carry a 'double burden of being labelled anti-national and appeased'; recommended an **Equal Opportunity Commission**, a **Diversity Index** and a **National Data Bank**. Follow-up: **Ranganath Misra Commission (2007)** recommended 15% reservation for minorities (10% for Muslims) — not implemented.

Examined **sub-categorisation of OBCs** under Article 340; found that about **97% of central OBC quota benefits went to just 25% of OBC castes**, and nearly **10% of the sub-castes got nothing at all**. Recommended splitting the 27% into sub-quotas. Report submitted in 2023, not yet made public — the parallel to *Davinder Singh* on SC sub-classification.

Second Backward Classes Commission (**B.P. Mandal**) — identified **3,743 castes** as OBC, estimated them at **52% of the population**, and recommended **27% reservation**, implemented in 1990 and upheld in *Indra Sawhney*. Preceded by the **Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953)**, the first Backward Classes Commission, whose report was not acted upon.

The blueprint of India's public health system — recommended **integration of preventive and curative services**, a **three-tier structure with primary health centres**, and 'no individual should fail to secure adequate medical care because of inability to pay'. The ancestor of PHCs, and of the National Health Mission.

items.t: National Commission on Population and the health committees
items.d: Health policy lineage: **Bhore (1946)** → **Mudaliar (1962, quality over expansion)** → **Srivastava (1975, community health workers → the ASHA idea)** → **National Health Policy 1983, 2002 and 2017**. NHP 2017's targets: **public health spending 2.5% of GDP by 2025**, life expectancy 70 by 2025, and 'Health and Wellness Centres' — now **Ayushman Arogya Mandirs**.

**University Education Commission (Radhakrishnan, 1948)**; **Secondary Education Commission (Mudaliar, 1952)**; **Kothari Commission (1964-66)** — the **10+2+3 structure**, the **common school system**, the **three-language formula** and **6% of GDP for education**; **National Policy on Education 1968 and 1986** (with the 1992 Programme of Action); **NEP 2020** — 5+3+3+3+4 structure, GER 50% by 2035, multidisciplinary institutions, **HECI as a single regulator with four verticals**, and mother-tongue instruction till at least Class 5.

**FSLRC (Justice B.N. Srikrishna, 2013)** — recommended a unified **Financial Sector Regulatory Framework**, a single **Financial Redress Agency**, and merging regulators; **Narasimham Committees (1991, 1998)** on banking reform; **P.J. Nayak Committee (2014)** on bank board governance and the **Banks Board Bureau**; **Damodaran Committee (2011)** on customer service.
